utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there were a few preliminary matters to be raised by the parties. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning. Regarding the additional pages from 65 ter 19777, the Prosecution yesterday used page 68 in B/C/S and 69 in English from that document; the diary of a Defence witness named Nenad Davidovic. The Prosecution has uploaded B/C/S pages 68 through 70, and English pages 69 through 71, of the diary, as well as the portions already admitted as P7418 under 65 ter 19777F.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mladic doesn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there seems to be a problem with the audio. Mr. Mladic, can you hear me now? Apparently not. Could the usher assist or could technicians assist. Can you hear me? Mr. Mladic, can you hear me now in a language you understand? I see your thumbs-up. Therefore, we'll proceed. Could I invite you to restart, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Regarding the additional pages from 65 ter 19777, the Prosecution yesterday used page 68 in B/C/S and 69 in English from that document, which is the diary of a Defence witness named Nenad Davidovic. The Prosecution has uploaded B/C/S pages 68 through 70 and English pages 69 through 71 of the diary, along with the portions already admitted as P7418 together under 65 ter 19777F. The three pages in each language represent what's clearly the notes of that meeting on June 24th that I'd inquired about. If the Defence have no objection, we request that the Court officer be instructed to assign P7418 to 65 ter 19777F.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw that Mr. Lukic was nodding in a sense that there is no objection. Madam Registrar, would you please replace the existing document known as P7418 by the new one under the number 65 ter 19777F, and the newly uploaded version is now admitted, still under the same number as P7418. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was informed that you had a few matters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And good morning, Your Honours. First, we would address our filing in regard of one of our 92 bis statements for Simic, Ljubisav. We filed it but we have to redact a few more portions because we spoke with the Prosecution yesterday, and they -- there was a dead-line for the Prosecution to respond to our motion and we agreed that we will withdraw this motion and file another one with the additional redactions, since there were some remarks in that statement that are directly in connection with the conduct of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, please assist me. Was the previous filing, was that a confidential one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the redactions are such that they do not touch upon confidentiality but rather on what is permitted under Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, there may be no need to put it under seal but rather to focus exclusively for purposes of this procedure on the new one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby on the record. We'll receive in due time a response by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Within two weeks after the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- files the new motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You can't respond before it's filed. That's understood. That was the Simic filing. Anything else, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We, as you ordered yesterday, we checked on this expertise by Mr. Gojkovic, and English version is missing only that one picture. That's the only discrepancy. But there were some differences in B/C/S. For example, somehow computer turned on page 2 in English there were numbers, 1 to 8; in B/C/S, there were bullet points. So we will change B/C/S now to have numbers. And there is one more page missing in B/C/S. It's -- in English, it's page 23. It's just situation plan for Petricevac church. Somehow that page was left out in B/C/S version. So that will be added in B/C/S version as the page 21a, so we have the same sequence of pages that we discussed on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, then, that we are dealing mainly with an administrative matter rather than any matter of substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, you're invited to upload all the correct versions, and we'll proceed meanwhile since it doesn't touch upon the substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the new version will be uploaded under number 1D05892A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see when it appears. Anything else? If not, the witness can be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I can inform the parties that Mr. Gojkovic yesterday provided not the USB stick itself because there were other files on it which are not relevant for this procedure, he considered them to be private. He was invited to have the relevant files copied onto another USB stick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there seems to be a problem with opening that file, but the new USB stick -- the USB stick on which the file was copied, it was only one file, has been handed over to one of the members of Chamber staff, and Chamber staff will seek the assistance of our technicians to see whether they can open that file, yes or no, and then it will be made available to the parties. Good morning, Mr. Gojkovic. I just informed -- can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic, I just explained to the parties that there was a follow-up yesterday afternoon where you were invited to provide files of earlier versions or at least versions of your report that you were hesitant to hand over the whole of the USB stick because there were files on it which are not relevant for us. Therefore, one file has been copied onto another USB stick which has been now handed over to Chamber staff. There were some problems in opening that file, and we are seeking assistance to have it opened. But if you could inform us in any way as to what format that file is so that we would be assisted in trying to open it, you're invited to give that information now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was all done in Word, A4 format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll see whether this Word file -- was it -- as far as you remember, was it a doc file or was it a docx file?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that. Some of -- parts of the documents were done in PDF, some documents I took from the internet. So there is a mixture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's all put together in one file. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see whether that assists. Then we'll now continue to hear your evidence. Mr. Lukic. But before we do so, Mr. Gojkovic, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Gojkovic. Good morning, Mr. Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we were talking about the mosque in Srebrenica, the destroyed mosque in Srebrenica. Do you have any information where the military units went after Srebrenica, and do you know how? This is after the action in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, although I wasn't really interested much in all of that, I know that the units set off towards Zepa immediately after Srebrenica. It's also -- it was also a safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when that was? If you don't, just say so and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the police station was set up in Srebrenica? Again, if you don't know just say so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at P7493.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown the document yesterday. It's from the command of the 1st Engineers Regiment, signed by Major Nastic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the next page. Only the part that was translated into English has been uploaded. We will ask that the whole document be translated. We have the whole document in front of us. I didn't know that it was uploaded in the way in which it was given to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I'm going to ask you this: When the engineering units were out in the field, how did they communicate with the units that they were resubordinated to or to whom they were providing support? Do you know what the communications were between the engineers units and these other units when they worked together?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in any case, the communication was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of communications you had? Was it radio communications, personal contacts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a combination. Mostly we went to the actual units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have radio communications with these units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We communicated exclusively through units to which our units were resubordinated, yes. In such cases, yes, but it was rare.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will find that in this blocked-out part of the document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I can just continue. There was the case of the Prnjavor Brigade to which we sent a pioneers platoon during the corridor operation. We could never bring that platoon back to us, the Prnjavor Brigade never allowed it to come back to our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I can see that my colleague is on his feet, so could you please just stop for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I've taken a moment on this line of questioning, Your Honour, but I don't see how it arises from my cross-examination and so I'd object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It arises from the document provided to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It arises from portions of the document that weren't tendered, that weren't used with the witness, and so doesn't arise from cross-examination, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless there's such a contextual issue that we could not stop reading where this document, which is not a complete document --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Unless -- right. Unless it relates to the portions that were used or tendered or to another topic from cross-examination, but I don't understand that to be the submission that Mr. Lukic made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is there any direct link to the cross-examination apart from that it's the same document? But is it, as far as the subject matter concerned, related?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is also one portion further in this document that will be directly linked to the portion we read yesterday, but we think that this is also crucial in understanding the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's not a matter of whether it's crucial to understand the situation in the field but rather whether it's linked to what was raised during cross-examination. It's not a reopening of your examination-in-chief. The Chamber has, of course, difficulties in evaluating what you said, because it was only the limited portion that was uploaded. And this leads me to another question. You said we have now the whole of the document before us. I see that the redacted document is three pages in B/C/S as uploaded, and the redaction on page number 3 goes to the very bottom of that. Does that mean that under the black part that we see -- as a matter of fact, we don't see that it's there, that the document ends?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I can assist. What we'd uploaded originally as the full version of the B/C/S was this full document and a couple of attachments to the document. What was admitted was just the portion that I used with the witness, and that's section 2, the Morale of Unit, and the cover page, just to reflect what the document is. So the original B/C/S, 32853 has, I think, 24 pages including the attachments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what is in a redacted format before us is not the whole of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is not the whole of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then you said there was another part which could be directly linked to cross-examination. If you would ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you announced that there was another portion which will be, as you said, directly linked to the portion you read yesterday. Is it -- were you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi read yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then tell us where it is, what it is, so that we can see whether it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. So Mr. Traldi was talking yesterday about forcible mobilisation of a big number of people, especially Muslims and Croats. And on page 7 in B/C/S, that's not translated, under number 6, which is Security, "Bezbednost." I will read the portion of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Extreme nationalism did not have any effect on our units. Members of both the Croatian and Muslim ethnic groups, for the most part, did not respond to the call up to the unit, but those who did respond initially mostly remained in the units."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic, do you know --

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about this and this remark is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Any mobilisation, by its very nature, is forceful?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any arrests, however, in your unit of Muslims and Croats who did not respond to the call up, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not a single Muslim or Croat was brought to the unit by force. As long as I was the commander, I assume afterwards as well when Milan Nastic was the commander and Stanko Vuckovic as well, it was the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we're not that much interested in assumptions, but I do understand that that's what the witness assumes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for this part that is in front of us and that has been translated, I am going to ask you something. Do not read. What was the material situation of the soldiers who were members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as equipment, explosives, et cetera, it was quite satisfactory. As far as uniforms are concerned, food, finance, it was miserable, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did people receive salaries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perhaps some individual companies that could ensure something for a certain number of soldiers, those who were better off, but most of the members of the unit did not receive any money whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, briefly now, how this functioned? People were in the army and you say some companies did make payments.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you had certain companies. I mean, all people who responded to call up had worked before that. There were some companies that were better off and that managed, in some way, to pay salaries to their employees. That kind of thing did happen. It's not that these were big salaries but they did receive some money. However, it was really a small number of soldiers, members of the unit, that were affected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since there is a reference here to the deteriorated materiel situation in this part that was translated, could you tell us about clothing, footwear, beds, bedding?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very poor. What can I tell you? I mean, if you have a situation when most of your soldiers hitch-hike to the front line and back, that is telling.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're done with this document, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question. This Chamber has heard evidence that Muslims and Croats were not always still employed by their companies and that some were fired or sent away. Do you know anything about whether Serbs, Muslims, and Croats were equally treated as far as payment by their companies is concerned? If you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they were a member of the unit, all were treated equally. It depended on the companies involved, how well off they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But was the situation in the companies, as far as continued employment is concerned, the same for all ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. The same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware or do you have any knowledge about some ethnicities not being able to continue to work in their companies, whereas others were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Everybody. All members of other ethnicities who happened to be in the army of Republika Srpska remained at their jobs. We never received any complaints from a single soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but apart from complaints do you have factual knowledge about Muslims, Croats, and Serbs being equally employed and continued to be employed by their companies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was discussed fairly often at briefings, and there were no such problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you something that was discussed rather extensively yesterday, and I must say that it remains unclear to me, even. You were asked how those 10 places of worship were destroyed in combat and 84 after the withdrawal of the JNA, how you made this distinction. You said that in Riedlmayer's report you found a source for that. Could you tell us -- could you explain this to us: On the basis of what did you draw these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the state of the building involved and the description that Riedlmayer provided in his report, and then I singled out Kotor Varos, Hambarine -- no, no. It's the mosque in Haradjani [phoen] in Kotor Varos, in Vecici Kotor Varos, the new mosque in Vecici Kotor Varos. It's the mosque Hadrovic [phoen] in Kotor Varos. It's the mosque in Prijedor. The Prijedor mosque in Cevici. It's Suceska mosque in Srebrenica, it is the Tokalici mosque in Srebrenica. It's the mosque in Sase in Srebrenica. It's the mosque in Vidikovac also in Srebrenica. And it's the town Catholic church also in Srebrenica. I worked on that basis. Had I had a bit more time -- the Trial Chamber objected that it was not done in detail, and had I had more time, I would have dealt with it in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in your question you referred to the withdrawal of the JNA. Did you mean JNA? I remember that we discussed yesterday the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- withdrawal of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But I take it that the witness understood it in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That you wanted to refer to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question here. Witness, the large number is destruction of religious building taking place after VRS withdrawal. That's, as you described it, for 84 buildings. Are you telling us that in Mr. Riedlmayer's report you would find whether or not at the time he assumed the buildings were destroyed that he gives information as to whether the VRS had withdrawn, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot say with certainty -- I mean, well, you see, maybe there were some soldiers who remained in a particular area. I cannot say anything. I didn't manage to analyse that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you whether you found that information in Mr. Riedlmayer's report for all of those 84 for which you said that they had been destroyed after VRS withdrawal. Whether Mr. Riedlmayer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- gives that information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So earlier I think you emphasized that whatever you found here was based on Mr. Riedlmayer's report. Now, if Mr. Riedlmayer's report does not contain information about VRS withdrawal, how for those 84 you could establish on the basis of Riedlmayer's report that the VRS had withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for these 10 buildings, Riedlmayer and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm talking about the 84 destroyed after VRS withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that -- let me tell you, as for these 10 buildings, Mr. Riedlmayer mentions them but the way in which other buildings were destroyed. I mean, there is no combat there. No nothing. He includes these 10 buildings at the time of combat, and that can be seen from the pictures. So if one says that in Cerici, in the Prijedor municipality, a minaret was targeted and it fell onto the building; that is to say, it was not blown up, it was targeted using other weapons, that's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, do I understand your testimony well that if Mr. Riedlmayer does not state that the destruction took place during combat operations that you assumed, more or less automatically, that the VRS had withdrawn when the building was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Riedlmayer doesn't write about that anywhere, and he doesn't draw any conclusions. He just takes statements from witnesses, and he takes information from the Islamic religious community. Riedlmayer never mentions anything like that. He doesn't draw any conclusions. He just transmits what he was told by others. So he did not devote himself to an analysis of that, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put a leading question, and I don't think that anybody will mind. The information that the VRS had withdrawn, that is your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And a conclusion based on what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That conclusion is based on the fighting simply stopping. That the units withdrew, that there were no war operations. Now, whether somebody was just milling about in order to loot, torch, that is something I cannot say. I cannot speak about that. I don't know. You know what? Everybody wears a uniform and then somebody who saw somebody in uniform doing something near a mosque and saying it's a soldier, well, that's very hard to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me then clearly ask you the following: You say once combat stops, you automatically assume that troops are not functional anymore in securing control over that area. Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's an answer. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just going to put one more question. Why do you draw that conclusion? On what basis?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have some experience. I spent four years in the war and I saw how units of the VRS operated. When Modrica was liberated, when -- well, I can't -- Kotor Varos, when Kotor Varos was liberated, the army withdrew immediately, automatically. They had nothing to do. What would they have to do? When the place was liberated, they would withdraw their equipment. And whether hyenas came in, doing whatever it was that they did, I cannot talk about that. I cannot testify about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just take one example, once, whether there was much combat or not, I leave that alone. But once -- as you express it, for example, Srebrenica was liberated, does that mean that all the troops disappeared from that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally think that they had nothing more to do. I mean, I don't know when it was that the leadership of the state appointed a president, when a government was set up. I cannot talk about that. I cannot testify about that. But I think that once combat operations are over, I don't see what the role of the army would be there. Only if there were to be a military administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned seven hours. You said that you worked on this for seven hours.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were paid to work for seven hours, but how long did you work personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about 140 hours, but then all my assistants -- so I think that the figure would be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It hasn't been recorded, how long your assistants?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked 130 hours. And the people I involved in this effort, I think that 500 hours would be the figure involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic, at page 18, line 21, you are recorded as having said that you worked 140 hours; and at page 19, line 3, you said 130 hours. Can you just tell us which is correct between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 140 hours. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when that was translated here in The Hague Tribunal, then it was 130 so then I said that. I mean, it's the Registry, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at 1D5894.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before it appears on our screens, you mentioned a conversation with Mr. Davidovic. Did you take a document from him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to him and I took a document that had to do with the destruction of the Ferhadija mosque in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We received that document late, so we didn't manage to translate it. It's a document of the Ministry of Religion of the government of Republika Srpska from 8th of May, 1995, and it says: "Announcement" --

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Lukic. This is a document from 1995, and it has to do with the destruction of the Petricevac monastery near Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see the signature, that was Minister Dragan Davidovic at the time, and you mentioned it in your testimony. Is that the document that you took from him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he told me then that he had the same sort of document for the two mosques that were destroyed in 1993 but he wasn't able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please just tell us what the gist of the document was? Is it -- does it indicate that the minister or the Ministry for Religion was in favour or against the destruction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely against. As is the case for the vast majority of the citizens of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would ask Your Honours to MFI this document, since there is no translation. And it was discussed yesterday during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the document was not discussed but the information received from the minister, I think, was -- Mr. Davidovic was something that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We have no objection to MFI'ing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5894 receives number D1184, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1184 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the last document I would like to show is P7496.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for it, could I ask the witness: The document which was on our screen a second ago only in the B/C/S version, did you provide that to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did it at the time when I was providing the Defence team in Banja Luka with documents, hard copies of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was that in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the 2nd of February, 2015.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's for quite a while in the hands of the Defence, I do understand. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown the document yesterday. It's an article from the "New York Times." An excerpt was read to you where Simo Drljaca says that you should not only knock down the minaret but also you need to shake the foundations of the mosque. Were you aware of the position of the authorities? Do you know what the position was of Mr. Karadzic, for example? We have that in this document and it wasn't read to you, but do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Karadzic, but I know about the reaction. I sat with Mr. Radic on a number of occasions. He was the president of the Banja Luka municipality at the current post of General Talic in Prnjavor, and I know that this was very strongly condemned. As for Mr. Simo Drljaca, his statement does not comport with the actual situation of the buildings that were destroyed in the field. This is his own story. He didn't actually implement on the ground what he's talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Neighbouring municipalities around Prijedor, were places of worship destroyed in those municipalities; do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I held the bridge across the river Sava from Jasenovac to Srbac in the municipality of Dubica in 1992, nothing was destroyed, in the Gradiska municipality nothing was destroyed, in Srbac, Laktasi municipalities, nothing was knocked down either. Banja Luka also. Except when I was the commander of the pontoon battalion, one Catholic building was torched in Topola, and I sent the military police there, then, to see what had happened, and I also provided security there until the people from the Gradiska MUP arrived. The first building that was destroyed in the territory of the municipality of Gradiska was sometime in February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will just ask you this. It's about the people under your command, Serbs, Muslims, Croats, other ethnic groups as well. What sort of training did they receive? Was there any difference in training of people from different ethnic groups in terms of their equipment, weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was all uniform. There was no difference. Again, I would like to say that the operations officer in my regiment was a Croat throughout the whole war. He was a really good officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please limit your answers to what is asked. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to show you the document. You were shown yesterday, some documents from the radical party paper, Vojislav Seselj's party. You were shown two cartoons. The text from this article as well as the activities of Dr. Seselj, what sort of influence did they have on the work of your unit? Did you read that paper, Zapadna Srbija?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never read the paper during the war. I never saw it. I don't remember its name. At the time, the work of the Serbian Radical Party was something that I was not interested at all, and ultimately General Mladic ordered that we were not permitted to be members of any political party. This was something that also was in force after the war. A witness of The Hague Tribunal -- I actually didn't know anything about the work of Dr. Vojislav Seselj, and I didn't know anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic, thank you very much. These were all the questions that we had for you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Traldi, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just very, very, briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Within five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Within five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we'll continue for those five minutes and then hear the next witness after the break. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Traldi:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, first, Mr. Lukic asked you this morning about salary payments to people in the 1st Krajina Corps' engineering units. You yourself received salary during the war from the VJ in Belgrade; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Through the 30th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So did the other officers who'd come over from the JNA to the VRS when the transformation occurred; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Finally, sir, this morning you were asked again about the distinction between mosques that you determined were destroyed during combat operations and mosques destroyed after VRS withdrawal. You said you assumed that when the combat operations were over the VRS left. Is it correct that you did not study any VRS documents to determine when VRS operations, setting aside whether they were combat or not, ended in a particular village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can show that best through an example: Fighting in Lisina, near -- well, in the Prnjavor municipality was conducted over a couple of days. Something like that. But the mosques were destroyed for months after that. It didn't happen in a single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, Lisina, that's not one of the mosques addressed in your report or Mr. Riedlmayer's; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I'm saying is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you could just let me go one step at a time, please, so we get this done quickly. When you give the explanation you just gave about Lisina, you're giving information you remember from when you were deployed in the Prnjavor area during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was while I was carrying out combat assignments, and I would pass by there, and then I could see when the mosques were destroyed. It was not -- they were not demolished all in one day. It took a period of time. The Prijedor mosques were --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking is about your methodology over the last couple of months or at the time the 630 hours spent on developing this report. During that period, for a village like Novoseoci or Rizvanovici or Ahatovici, is it correct that you reviewed no VRS documents during the preparation of the report to determine when VRS operations in that village had ended?

utterances.speaker: DRAGIC GOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My methodology, Mr. Prosecutor, was more or less the same as that of Mr. Riedlmayer. I could not rely on anything else --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're not invited to compare your methodology with that of Mr. Riedlmayer. The simple question was whether you systematically, and I heard the word "systematically," reviewed documents as to whether after combat was over, whether operations of whatever kind by the VRS continued and whether you studied that on the basis of documentary evidence. I see you are nodding no, that you did not. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried. But at the time I could not have access to any documents. I went to the archives, but I could get none of the documents, so I exclusively relied on the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I've no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if the witness can just take off his headphones please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones for a second, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours want to check it with the witness, in the document that was redacted and translated only in a small portion, which is P7493, it is mentioned how many active-duty officers were in that unit. It's at 1.4, when it was discussed about salaries received from the Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I -- if Mr. Lukic has the e-court page, I'd appreciate it. I don't understand what 1.4 officers are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not in the e-court, because you put only two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, the e-court for 65 ter 32853 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- is the full document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's page 13 of 65 ter 32853. And it says "active duty officers, reserve," and total number of soldiers. So you will see active-duty officers, 1.4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're drawing our attention to a portion of the documentary evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what we ask -- we will ask for this document to be translated in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd say we'll find most likely information in that document --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which is not visible for us at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And 1.5 is officers, commissioned officers, and soldiers in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we're -- at this moment, we are discussing the content of the evidence, and I think that's not appropriately done at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I asked for the witness to take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll see once we have before us the whole of the document. Parties have ample opportunity to argue about it and what it tells us or what it doesn't tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I agree. And, as always, we're open to Mr. Lukic suggesting any additional portions from the document he's interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Mr. Lukic, can the witness put on his earphones again?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he can. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness. Mr. Gojkovic, the parties have no further questions for you. Neither has the Bench. Which means that we are at the end of hearing your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you. You're excused. You may follow the usher, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We spend so much time together it's easy to misplace us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't call you identical twins yet, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Perhaps I was flattering myself. Just to ensure that we have the right people here at the beginning of the next session, Your Honour, I know the tendering of the report remains pending. But because we're still awaiting the Word document, I wonder if we might postpone that until we have ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see from Mr. Lukic nodding that he doesn't disagree or even agrees. Further time will be given for the tendering of the report and any objections to it. We take a break and will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are. We are calling Ms. Bosiljka Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Mladic, I assume. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make the solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Ms. Mladic. Ms. Mladic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mrs. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, could you please slowly state your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Bosiljka Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mladic, at one point in time did you give a statement to members of the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see 1D1749 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the English version here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. What you're looking at is the transcript, and on the other screen you will see your statement. Mrs. Mladic, there is a document before us. Do you see a signature there?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see a signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is written in your statement, does that correspond to what you said to the members of the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, what is contained in the statement, is it correct and truthful?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct and truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you give me the same answers?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would tender the statement of Mrs. Mladic into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any summary for the public?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will read the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, Ms. Hasan? Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1749 receives number D1185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1185 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will read a short summary, a very short summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mladic is our alibi witness in connection of the whereabouts of Mr. Mladic from 14th to 17th of July, 1995, and Ms. Mladic, Bosiljka, is General Mladic's wife. She will testify that in the period from 14th until 17th of July, 1995 General Mladic was in Belgrade along with her, and she will provide details on General Mladic's whereabouts on those dates. This is a short summary. And I will, with your leave, Your Honours, have several questions for Mrs. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Mladic, in your statement you refer to the dates of the 14th, 15th, and 16th, and the morning of the 17th of July, 1995. This is what I'm going to ask you now: Your husband, General Ratko Mladic, where was he during the night between the 14th and 15th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: He was at home with me in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your husband, General Mladic, where was he during the night between the 15th and 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: He was with me at home in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your husband, General Mladic, what was he during the night between the 16th and 17th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: He was at home with me in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How do you know that General Mladic spent the night at home?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: I know because we were preparing for a wedding on the 16th of July. He arrived in the evening, in the evening hours, and he immediately reminded me that we need to prepare for this wedding. So I remember those days. He -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go to sleep together?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes. We went to sleep together, we had dinner together, we got up together, we had breakfast, had coffee, talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those days, while you were with General Mladic between the 14th and the morning of the 17th, did you notice that he had some kind of communications equipment? Did he have a radio, a Motorola, or something?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: No, he had none of that. He just wore his uniform when he entered the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see Mladjo Kenjic or anybody else who was escorting General Mladic? Did they have any communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: No, I did not notice any communications equipment on anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the statement, you said that at one moment you travelled by car and that Mladjo Kenjic drove you. In the car where you were riding with General Mladic, did you see any communications equipment, a radio or something?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: When we were going to the wedding, it was Mladjo Kenjic who was driving us, and there was no communications equipment in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see your husband, General Mladic, during those days that he was using any communications equipment, either his own or somebody else's?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I mean, even before when he would come, he did not do that, and this time he didn't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mladic, thank you. That is all that the Defence have for you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Ms. Mladic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Hasan. You'll find Ms. Hasan to your right. Ms. Hasan is counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Hasan, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: When was it that you married Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: We got married on the 24th of April, 1966.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So am I right that you will have just had your 49th wedding anniversary?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: When was it that you first learned that the Tribunal here in The Hague had issued an indictment against your husband?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: It would be perhaps in 1996, 1997 that I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, I can imagine that that's a pretty significant event, to learn that criminal charges for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity are being laid against your husband. You don't even remember the year, whether it was 1996, 1997?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: No, I really cannot recall when it was that I first heard about that. But I think it was 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: When you learned that, I take it you were afraid for your husband?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you didn't want to see anything bad happen to him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You certainly didn't want to see -- don't want to see your husband convicted for any of these crimes, do you?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Well, I am sure that he could not have committed such crimes, and that is why I believe that he does not deserve to be convicted. Otherwise, I condemn any crime, even if it were committed by my husband.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: When was the last time you were in touch with your husband before he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: When was the last time you were in touch with your husband before he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of June, 2001. I think the day when President Milosevic was arrested. My husband was at home and soon, a couple of hours later, he left the house, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you formed the belief that your husband was dead, isn't that right, at some point after he left?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Well, I was convinced because he had had strokes in 1996, as far back as that. So we were thinking we hadn't heard from him, about him, for a long time, and that is why we thought that. And later on when he was arrested, it became obvious that he was in a very difficult state.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, you refer to "we." Who are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: When I said "we," I said "we believed that he was sick and that he was not alive," is that it? When I'm saying that, I'm referring to myself and my son.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And when was it then that you first formed the belief that your husband was dead?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? As I was thinking -- because I knew what his condition was, and we thought that he was living a hard life. And it's not that I saw something specific or heard something specific, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: But at some point you started to believe that your husband was no longer alive. When was that?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Well, say, 2011.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The same year that he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So up until --

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe not that much. I don't know. Maybe half a year before that. I really cannot remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So about half a year before 2011. Until that point in time, Mrs. Mladic, you believed your husband -- you knew your husband to be alive?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: I assumed so. I couldn't be sure. The man had left, many years had passed, a whole decade, and that was the thinking of me and my son. Because a lot of time had gone by, and he wasn't in very good health when he left.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, in December of 2008 the authorities in Belgrade found weapons in a closet in your home, in your apartment in Belgrade. That's right?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You were charged with the illegal possession of weapons?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And those charges were eventually withdrawn, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I won the dispute.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, Mrs. Mladic, isn't it the case that the charges were withdrawn? There was no verdict at the end of the trial?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: There was no verdict and the court charges were covered by the state. I didn't have to pay for the cost of the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And when I'm -- you may have misunderstood me. When I say the charges were eventually withdrawn, I mean the -- I'm talking about the allegations that were made against you.

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I don't understand the terminology that well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try and clarify. The criminal allegations that were brought against you for the illegal possession of the arms, those allegations were dropped? The prosecution decided not to pursue that further? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, so that's why I'm saying -- well, all right. You could put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on now. You told the court in Belgrade that you had no idea what was in that cupboard. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And why was it that you didn't open the cupboard to see what was in there?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: I did open it because I knew that there were things of his in there. He's an officer, and if he tells us not to touch anything in there, that's what we do. We don't touch anything in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And "he," you're referring to your husband, Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, my husband, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And he told you not to touch anything in the cupboard. When did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot remember the date, but that was during the period when he was at home, when he would come home from time to time. And for a long time still the state was providing the security.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So we're talking about before the last time you saw him in 2001. When you say "it was when he would come from time to time," are you talking about from the wartime or are you talking about after that?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And did he tell you before he left in 2000 -- or six months before -- sorry. In 2001, did he tell you not to touch what was in that cupboard?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: No, not then. He didn't say then. We knew before that time that we weren't supposed to touch it. But he got ready hastily and he left the house, and then after that, he didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Up until the apartment was searched in 2008, Mrs. Mladic, you complied with your husband's instructions not to open the cupboard. That's what you claim?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So one can say that you are faithful to your husband?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Look, I have spent my whole life with my husband. Since the time he was a second-lieutenant to a general, as an officer, and even before, he would bring things home. And then if he said, "Please don't touch that," both myself and the children would respect that. We wouldn't touch it if he told us not to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And this despite his absence over many, many years?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Mladic, did you discuss the substance of your testimony here today with anyone?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke with the lawyer. Just the lawyer, not anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And when you mention "the lawyer," you're talking about Mr. Mladic's Defence team? Is that who you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He just said that he had my statement, he gave it to me, and I have the statement with me now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And who was it that first contacted you regarding the details of your husband's activities between the 14th and the 17th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Nobody contacted me. I was summoned sometime in July 2014 to give a statement, so I gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Mladic, do you recall that -- now you're referring here to being summoned in July 2014 to give this statement that we've looked at here today.

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, my question is --

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: My question was when was it that you first were contacted about the activities - your activities and your husband's activities - between the 14th and 16th of July, 1995? Was that the first time -- that wasn't actually the first time you had been contacted in regards to that, was it?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: That was the first time that I was contacted regarding that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Right. So you don't remember being contacted by the war crimes department in Belgrade in 2012 regarding these dates? You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes. No, no. You have just reminded me that I was called once. I really couldn't remember right away. I'm trying to remember now the -- the date. Yes, you are correct. But I really cannot remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It was a long time ago, so you don't remember; isn't that right, Mrs. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was much earlier. I can't remember, but it was before 2014.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Mladic, what is it that you remember -- or what is it that you were told about the significance of these days that you were asked about by the war crimes department and the high court in Belgrade as well as by the Defence of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: They asked me whether he was at home during those days, the 14th, the 15th, and the 16th of July. I think that was the gist of it. Perhaps there was some other questions, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Were you told why they were interested in those dates?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I take it that means you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: No, no. I really cannot remember. I can't say anything that wouldn't be ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Mrs. Mladic, you certainly were aware that during those dates that you were asked about, that thousands of Bosnian Muslim men and boys were executed after the fall of Srebrenica? You were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: I heard about some things from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: When did you first hear about these atrocities?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Perhaps again 2000-something, when things started happening. I mean, we had some information about the events, when it was happening. There were some things shown on TV. Then later in 2000 -something, there was a propaganda that started that it was just the Serbs who had committed the crime, that it was a major crime. So I think in 2000-something this propaganda started appearing. It was in the media, it was in newspapers, on television, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mrs. Mladic, now, you told us that you knew that your husband had been indicted sometime in either 1996 or 1997, and you didn't at any point ask what those crimes were?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: I did. I did when I started to listen to all of those things which, in my opinion, was propaganda, and we heard some things earlier that were completely different during the war. And at one point I asked him, "Ratko, please tell me the truth. Did you issue any order regarding these crimes that happened in Srebrenica?" And at that point, he got very serious and he looked at me sharply, and he said, "Are you doubting me?"

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, in fact, Mrs. Mladic, you did understand at the time you learned about the indictment that there had been serious and grave crimes that had been committed after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Like I said, I was following this in the media. I was reading about it. Some people said it was a very high number; for example, General MacKenzie wrote in the Novosti newspaper that it couldn't be so, it couldn't be that many, if crimes did occur, they were at a much smaller scale, and so on. I knew that some crime was committed. That's why I asked him about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, it has been many years since then. Do you accept that over 7.000 Muslim men and boys were massacred?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: No, I don't accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the base for this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's just a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's -- that's the question. Apparently whether the witness accepts what was alleged to have happened. That's, at least I take it Ms. Hasan, that that's what your question was about. The witness has answered the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, how long did it take you, when you were asked about the events between 14 and 17 July, did it take you to remember the details of those dates?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Well, look: I didn't need a lot of time because that was the first time that he was in Belgrade for three days. Secondly, there was this wedding. In the evening before, he said that there would be this wedding. In the morning, the following day, there was a difficult moment for me. We had also lost our daughter. I was still wearing black in mourning. And then before he went off for a meeting, he told me, "Buy a pretty dress." And this is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, Mrs. Mladic, now you said you didn't need a lot of time, okay, to remember. So you remember the details --

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, because of those moments.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let me finish. Okay. So when you were asked about this, you immediately remembered the details of what took place on those dates? You didn't --

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? Where were things happening? I don't understand the question. What do you mean? You mean the things that happened in Belgrade or the things that were happening in Srebrenica? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let me clarify. When you were asked about what took place between the 14th and the 17th of July, I understood you to be saying that you --

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just let me finish the question. I understood you to be saying that it didn't take you a lot of time to remember the details of what took place; is that correct? It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: What was happening during these days, you mean; on the 14th, the 15th, and the 16th of July. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it should be -- sorry, sorry. Stop --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I didn't need a lot of time for those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment. Could you please stop for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness asked that question specifies where. That was confusion. Where: Srebrenica or Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you clarified, Ms. Hasan, I think you are not that clear in clarifying what the witness asked. And I think, Mrs. Mladic -- but please correct me when I'm wrong, Ms. Hasan, that how much time it took to remember what happened in those days, that you are constantly referring to what happened in Belgrade during those days. Is that what you intended to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said, Mrs. Mladic, that you didn't need a lot of time for those days, you were referring for that you didn't need a lot of time to remember what happened during those days in Belgrade. Is that how we have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the matter has been clarified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So in the process of responding to the questions put to you by the high court in Belgrade, the war crimes department, and by, well, initially by them, you didn't have to consult in advance of that with anybody? You didn't talk to anyone, you didn't talk to --

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't talk to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement that you -- and this is at paragraph 2 of your statement, that you remember -- you say: "I remember my spouse, Ratko Mladic, coming home in the evening hours of 14 July ..." So that's when you recall he arrived from Bosnia; that's right?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That he arrived, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you remember what day of the week the wedding was?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: No. No, I cannot confirm the day. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Just so we're all on the same page, whose wedding was it that you attended?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: It was the wedding of Biljana Djurdjevic and Zarko Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Right. So going back to the evening of the 14th of July when you say your husband arrived from Bosnia, you say he came in the evening hours. What time did he arrive?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the time exactly, but he came sometime early in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And early in the evening is approximately what time? Give me an hour.

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say that it was about 7.00, 7.00 and a bit. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Mladic, when you gave your -- when you answered a question before the high court in Belgrade in March of 2012, you swore to tell the truth, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And after answering questions in the courtroom, a statement was compiled, it was read to you, you said you had no objections to it, and you signed it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: The statement you mean? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, let's look at that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 32878.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This is the record of the witness interview compiled on 19 March 2012 before the judge for preliminary proceedings of the high court in Belgrade, war crimes department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Mladic, before the next question will be put to you, apparently you have some paper before you. Could you tell us what papers? Is that your own statement as given to the Defence, or is it anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the statement that I gave to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So you see here the front page.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we can just turn to page 2 in the English and 3 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's your signature there, Mrs. Mladic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSILJKA MLADIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to look at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
